title: Chip-mediated manipulation of photonic quantum skyrmions
abstract: Quantum skyrmions are attracting much interest owing to their topological robustness, which offers a route to address noise and loss in quantum systems. The toolkit for their creation has advanced recently, enabling quantum skyrmions to be generated in bulk systems as entangled states and on chip as single-photon states. However, methods for generating on-chip entangled skyrmions, as well as for their reconfigurable manipulation and controlled interfacing with single-photon skyrmions, remain elusive. Here we demonstrate entangled skyrmions and their manipulation on chip with an integrated silicon nitride nanophotonic platform. The skyrmion topology is coherently encoded in a local single-photon spin-textured quantum state, which is subsequently transferred into a non-local skyrmion topology shared between two entangled photons. Throughout the transfer process, the topology remains preserved under background noise and different types of disturbance, even after the entanglement vanishes. This establishes a quantum-topology-enabled transfer scheme beyond entanglement, which reveals a fundamentally enhanced resilience that outperforms conventional entanglement-assisted quantum state transfer. This approach serves as a step towards building robust quantum interconnects and advancing distributed quantum information technology mediated by topology.

title: Morphogenesis of a stratified cell mound at a vortex defect
abstract: Topological defects in cell monolayers have been recognized as mechanical organizing centres in morphogenetic processes. However, the mechanism by which cells coordinate their motion at such defects and self-organize into higher order structures remains elusive. Here we describe the formation of three-dimensional multicellular mounds in unconfined myoblast monolayers at well-controlled vortex topological defects. Before the onset of the formation of a bilayer, the vortex structure induces millimetre-scale cell flows that converge towards the defect centre. As a result, three-dimensional cell mounds form at the defect core, layer by layer. These mounds grow by interlayer permeation sustained by the converging cell flows. At late stages, the bell shape of the structured mounds can be modelled with dynamics driven by these converging flows. Our results highlight the crucial role of integer topological defects in driving large-scale cell flows that result in the formation of highly ordered three-dimensional tissues from a monolayer. We propose that similar mechanisms may be at play in certain morphogenetic and tumorigenic events.

title: SESAME could unlock more opportunities
abstract: Higher education institutions in the Middle East are not yet making the most of the synchrotron light source in Jordan.

title: Fusion digital twins from imperfect models
abstract: Digital twins could transform how fusion plasmas are predicted, designed and controlled. We argue that realizing this promise requires multi-fidelity frameworks that systematically combine imperfect models and data while quantifying uncertainty.

title: A dynamic ruler for positional memory in regeneration
abstract: Zebrafish can determine the amount of tissue to regrow after appendage amputation. Now, a study shows that a signal gradient that scales with the amount of tissue left to regenerate ensures that an amputated tailfin regrows to the correct length.

title: Reaction–diffusion competition drives anomalous relaxation of vitrimers
abstract: Since their discovery in 2011, vitrimers—covalent associative network polymers—have challenged the traditional understanding of soft matter relaxation dynamics. Unlike typical glass-forming liquids, the viscous relaxation of vitrimers can be entirely decoupled from their underlying structural dynamics. In addition, the origin of the Arrhenius viscosity in vitrimers in the presence of super-Arrhenius structural relaxation behaviour has been of high interest due to its potential to provide readily reprocessable high-performance plastics. Here we identify two types of transient networks in the relaxation dynamics of vitrimers based on the ratio of atomic displacement scales required for bond exchange to those required to relax a segment. In systems where bond exchange requires only subsegmental motion, our results indicate that network relaxation is governed by a competition between chemical exchange reactions and segmental diffusion. This competition produces the signature network–segment decoupling of the vitrimers and also drives a commonly observed crossover between Arrhenius and super-Arrhenius behaviour. This suggests an explanation for long-standing puzzling features of vitrimer dynamics and establishes a foundation for rational vitrimer design.

title: Monolayer van der Waals kagome lattice for high-temperature flat-band physics
abstract: Kagome lattice materials host a variety of intriguing quantum phenomena arising from the intrinsic interplay of topology, electron correlations and geometric frustration. Even though previous studies have primarily focused on bulk three-dimensional kagome materials, the realization of an ideal two-dimensional kagome system has remained a long-standing goal. Here we demonstrate ideal two-dimensional monolayer kagome lattices in the van der Waals material family A 2 T 3 X 4 , where A is an alkali metal, T is a transition metal and X is a chalcogen. Our nanofocused angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy directly characterizes the electronic structure of A 2 T 3 X 4 down to the monolayer limit, revealing an isolated kagome-derived flat band just below the Fermi level. Through electrostatic gating, the kagome flat band can be further tuned to the Fermi level, enabling direct access to partially filled flat-band physics. Compared with existing moiré-based artificial flat-band systems, this monolayer kagome platform realizes more than 220-fold higher flat-band electron density, offering opportunities to explore emergent flat-band phenomena at temperatures higher than those currently achievable.

title: Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array
abstract: Silicon spin qubits offer a promising path to scalable quantum computing due to their compatibility with industrial semiconductor manufacturing. A key requirement for scaling quantum processors is the ability to perform high-fidelity operations in parallel across many qubits. However, simultaneous control remains a major challenge in silicon devices, as fidelities typically degrade under parallel operation. Here we identify microwave-drive-induced a.c.-Stark shifts as the dominant source of this degradation in a five-qubit silicon spin array. We address this by introducing a scalable mitigation protocol based solely on pairwise phase calibrations. Using tailored control pulses on a shared control line, we achieve primitive X and Y gate fidelities well above 99.99% for each qubit individually, with some approaching 99.999%. Furthermore, these fidelities are preserved above 99.99% during simultaneous operation of up to three qubits. During parallel five-qubit operation, fidelities remain above the widely targeted fault-tolerant threshold of 99.9%. By maintaining high-fidelity control during simultaneous operation, shared qubit-control lines can support the development of large-scale semiconductor quantum processors.

title: Cavity-less Brillouin strong coupling in a solid-state continuous system
abstract: Strong coupling between two systems allows them to exchange coherent information before the systems decohere. This important regime in light–matter interactions has predominantly been reached in optical resonator configurations. Here we demonstrate strong coupling between optical and acoustic fields within a continuum of modes in a cavity-less configuration after a single pass through an optical waveguide. The underlying physical effect of anti-Stokes Brillouin–Mandelstam scattering in a highly nonlinear fibre at cryogenic temperature allows us to experimentally demonstrate strong coupling in a waveguide scenario. We show the splitting of the optoacoustic spectral response and introduce a technique to measure the avoided crossing of hybrid optoacoustic modes via forced detuning. This demonstration opens a path towards in-line acoustic-wave-based quantum signal processing in waveguide systems.

title: The extraction of work from hidden degrees of freedom
abstract: Thermodynamics establishes that information acquired through measurement can be converted into work, as exemplified by Maxwell’s demon and Szilard engines. Most experimental realizations of information engines, however, implicitly assume Markovian environments, in which information exchanged with the surroundings is irreversibly lost. Many physical systems instead exhibit environmental memory, with hidden degrees of freedom retaining correlations with the history of the system and giving rise to non-Markovian dynamics. Whether and how such concealed memory can be harnessed as a thermodynamic resource has remained an open question. Here we experimentally demonstrate the extraction of work from environmental memory. Using time-resolved measurements on an optically trapped Brownian particle in equilibrium, we implement a time-delayed double-measurement protocol that retrieves information through backflow from hidden bath degrees of freedom. We show that this information backflow alters the relaxation dynamics, can be quantified independently of initial state effects and—when appropriately exploited—enhances work extraction. Notably, we identify regimes in which the extracted work exceeds the energy stored in the observable degree of freedom alone. Our results establish environmental memory as an experimentally accessible thermodynamic resource and reveal how non-Markovian dynamics can be systematically explored to improve the performance of information engines operating in time-correlated environments.

title: Chaos control with broken symmetries
abstract: By breaking both material and cavity symmetries, waves can be funnelled into robust closed-loop patterns. This dual-symmetry-breaking approach enables the development of a new class of devices for wave-based signal processing and sensing.

title: Evidence for spin-fluctuation-mediated superconductivity in electron-doped cuprates
abstract: In conventional, phonon-mediated superconductors, the transition temperature and the linear-in-temperature normal-state scattering rate are linked through the electron–phonon coupling strength. In cuprate high-temperature superconductors, no equivalent relationship between critical temperature and electron–boson coupling has been identified. Here we highlight such a link with electrons scattering off commensurate antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations of variable strength. We use d.c. resistivity and high-field magnetoresistance to extract the scattering rate in electron-doped La 2− x Ce x CuO 4 as a function of doping. We reveal a highly anisotropic inelastic component to the scattering rate whose magnitude diminishes markedly as doping increases. The correlation we highlight between the strength of scattering and the critical temperature then identifies low-energy spin fluctuations as the primary pairing glue in electron-doped cuprates. The contrasting magnetotransport behaviour in hole-doped cuprates suggests that the higher critical temperature in those materials cannot be attributed solely to an increase in the coupling strength to the antiferromagnetic fluctuations. The success in modelling La 2− x Ce x CuO 4 reinforces the notion that resolving the origin of high-temperature superconductivity in hole-doped cuprates may require more than a simple extension of the Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer theory.

title: A liquid-crystal analogue of the skyrmion Hall effect
abstract: Topology provides a unifying framework across disciplines, ranging from particle physics and cosmology to condensed-matter systems. In condensed matter, one of its most striking manifestations is the skyrmion Hall effect, where skyrmions—emergent spin configurations characterized by a conserved topological charge—acquire a transverse velocity under driving. Recent advances have revealed that chiral liquid crystals host a wide variety of topological solitons, including torons and skyrmion tubes. Here we show that such solitons exhibit a Hall-like response under shear flow, undergoing a transverse drift away from the shear direction. Our theoretical analysis predicts a weak net transverse mass flow whose magnitude scales as the cube of the shear rate. However, tracer-particle experiments and numerical simulations show that the solitons do not behave as passive tracers of this flow: their transverse motion is much stronger, and in simulations, it occurs opposite to the net transverse mass current. A liquid-crystal analogue of the Thiele equation provides a simple physical framework that highlights the central role of flow vorticity in the effect. These results establish a liquid-crystal analogue of the skyrmion Hall effect and open pathways for microfluidic technologies that exploit soft topological solitons as functional building blocks.

title: Fibres and glasses are competing material states in protein condensation
abstract: Dense, well-ordered material states of proteins form the amyloid fibres that are indicative of neurodegenerative disease in the brain. In addition to forming amyloid fibres, some of these proteins comprise condensates that are initially liquid-like but evolve to a glassy, solid-like phase. Fibre growth requires a large supply of monomers, and so it is often speculated that fibres emerge from within a dense condensate as it ages and its microscopic dynamics slow into a glassy state. Here we show that, in the model system Fused in Sarcoma (FUS), fibres grow overwhelmingly in the dilute phase surrounding the condensates; concurrently, the condensates evolve to a glassy arrested solid. The resulting protein fibres and glassy condensates are both distinct solid-like phases that coexist but do not directly interconvert. These findings suggest that there may be two competitive ageing pathways in FUS condensation that are linked through phase separation kinetics.

title: Light-induced asymmetric pseudogap below the critical temperature in cuprates
abstract: High-temperature cuprate superconductors remain a key platform for studying the competition and coexistence of emergent quantum phases of matter. These include non- s -wave superconductivity with a high transition temperature, non-Fermi-liquid transport and the pseudogap regime. How superconductivity emerges alongside and competes with the pseudogap remains an open question. Here, by directly accessing the near-antinodal region of optimally doped Bi-based cuprates via time- and angle-resolved photoemission, we report a transient change from a symmetric superconducting-like density of states to an asymmetric pseudogap-like density of states when superconductivity is disrupted by a sufficiently high excitation fluence. We observe this change at electronic temperatures well below the equilibrium superconducting critical temperature. Conversely, when superconductivity is fully restored, the pseudogap is suppressed, as indicated by a particle–hole-symmetric density of states. We also observe the coexistence of pseudogap and superconducting features at intermediate times or intermediate fluence. Our findings challenge the view that superconductivity emerges from phase coherence in the pseudogap. Instead, we show that the two states compete and that the low-temperature ground state of cuprates reflects an interplay between the superconducting and pseudogap states.

title: Superconductivity and ferroelectric orbital magnetism in semimetallic rhombohedral hexalayer graphene
abstract: Rhombohedral multilayer graphene has become a platform for exploring correlated and topological quantum phases, enabled by its flat bands that carry Berry curvature. However, previous studies have mainly focused on separated conduction and valence bands. Here we study the semimetallic regime of rhombohedral hexalayer graphene in which the conduction and valence bands overlap. We reveal a rich phase diagram dominated by flavour-symmetry breaking, featuring correlated insulators, several pockets of superconductivity and two distinct multiferroic orbital magnetic orders. Near a band inversion, we observe two superconducting-like states confined to regions with coexisting electron and hole Fermi surfaces, suggesting a possible dual-carrier origin. Additionally, we identify a ferroelectric orbital magnetic state that undergoes sharp switching under unipolar electric fields, which signals spontaneous electric polarization. Unlike previously reported multiferroicity near zero electric field, this state exhibits magnetic hysteresis reversible by electric field, consistent with a phenomenological model of coupled electric and magnetic polarization. Our work elucidates the correlated semimetal regime in rhombohedral graphene and underscores its potential to host diverse quantum phases.

title: Coherent phonon control beyond amplitude saturation in a sliding ferroelectric
abstract: The breakdown of Hooke’s law marks the onset of nonlinear behaviour: when displacements become large, restoring forces weaken and Hookean proportionality fails. In quantum materials, intense optical excitation can drive the crystal lattice into a similar regime, where established linear relations between light, electrons and phonons no longer hold. Displacive excitation of coherent phonons, the principal mechanism for launching structural motion, typically assumes that lattice-driving forces scale linearly with the photo-excited carrier density. At high excitation, however, this linearity can break down, which fundamentally limits accessible lattice displacements. Here we show that such nonlinear limitations can be surpassed in a sliding ferroelectric by timing, rather than strengthening the optical drive. Time-resolved second-harmonic generation reveals that the interlayer-sliding phonon governing ferroelectricity saturates and even diminishes under single-pulse excitation. By means of first-principles calculations, we attribute this nonlinearity to band-specific electron–phonon coupling that induces competing forces on the lattice. By splitting the optical energy into two well-timed pulses that avoid populating counteracting states, we achieve markedly larger phonon amplitudes at fixed total fluence. The resulting enhanced sliding motion exposes a regime of anharmonic phonon coupling that emerges only far from equilibrium.

title: Teleportation transition of surface codes on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: The surface code is a leading candidate for harnessing long-range entanglement to protect logical quantum information against errors, and teleportation of the code’s logical states is desirable for robust quantum information processing. However, large numbers of physical qubits are needed to produce well-protected logical states, making quantum teleportation a formidable experimental challenge. Here we demonstrate the teleportation of surface code states with code distances up to 7, implemented on a superconducting quantum processor with 125 qubits. We obtain a phase diagram for successful teleportation of the logical state by tuning the local entangling gates uniformly across a finite threshold. Furthermore, we show that the entangling threshold can be boosted by coherent qubit rotations that inject non-classical magic resources, restoring the duality symmetry of the surface code’s topological phase. This serves as a guiding principle to minimize the entanglement needed to achieve many-body teleportation. Our results establish the potential for surface code teleportation to enable distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Wigner crystals get dressed
abstract: When repulsion overcomes their tendency to move freely, electrons can arrange into a crystal. Two experiments have now identified Wigner polarons, quasiparticles whose optical signatures reveal the collective response of the electron lattice.

title: Beating the break-even point with autonomous quantum error correction
abstract: Quantum error correction protects fragile quantum information by encoding it in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces. Conventional protocols typically require repeated syndrome measurements, real-time feedback or post-selection, and multiple physical qubits, which add technical complexity. Here we realize autonomous quantum error correction with a logical qubit encoded in multiple internal spin states of a single trapped ion and surpass the break-even point for qubit lifetime. We use engineered spin–motion couplings to transfer error-induced entropy into motional modes, which is then dissipated by sympathetic cooling with an ancilla ion. This eliminates the need for measurement and feedback. By repeatedly applying this protocol, we observe lifetime extension under both ambient laboratory conditions and injected low-frequency magnetic noise. Our results show that the multilevel structure of trapped ions can support hardware-efficient quantum error correction and robust quantum memories with reduced overhead.

title: Particle collisions on a quantum computer
abstract: Elementary particle physics rests on the discovery of particles produced in high-energy collider experiments. Now, a model collision above the threshold for particle production has been simulated on a quantum computer.

title: Maxwell’s demon with memory
abstract: Maxwell’s demon may produce work using the information it obtains by measuring the system as fuel. Now, it is shown that the amount of produced work increases if the demon takes information about the dynamical correlations of the system into account.

title: Three-dimensional cell morphology is mediated by curvature sensing and interfacial stress
abstract: Curvature sensing of cells critically governs three-dimensional cell morphology, which is integral to tissue and organ development as well as the wound-healing processes. However, the underlying mechanism by which sensing occurs remains unclear. Here we investigate the physical principles that govern curvature sensing at both single-cell and monolayer levels. We find that the cell–substrate interfacial stress ratio—defined as the balance between the cell contractile stress and the cell–substrate adhesion stress—determines the two predominant three-dimensional cell morphology modes, namely, complete adhesion and partial interior detachment. When the interfacial stress ratio is much higher than unity, a rapid morphological shift from complete adhesion to partial interior detachment occurs. This process is irreversible, as it proceeds towards a lower-energy state. We observe this mode switching for various cell types, under pharmacological perturbations and across multicellular layers, offering a universal biophysical framework for regulating three-dimensional cell morphology.

title: A simple twist to altermagnetism
abstract: Two-dimensional altermagnets hold promise for next-generation spintronics but remain difficult to synthesize. Now, altermagnetism has been observed in an orthogonally twisted van der Waals homostructure, opening possibilities for ultrathin devices.

title: Curvature and cell mechanics control tissue organization
abstract: Tissue geometry mechanically regulates cell behaviour across scales. Now, it can be predicted when cells switch from full adhesion to rapid partial detachment on curved surfaces.

title: Order in a quantum chaotic sea
abstract: Experiments with a superconducting quantum processor revealed an island of regular motion within otherwise chaotic quantum many-body dynamics and used feedback to steer the dynamics towards it.

title: Imaging hot-electron Thomson cooling beyond the Boltzmann–Onsager framework
abstract: Classical Thomson cooling, constrained by lattice-dominated heat dissipation and the weak entropy variation of charge carriers under thermal equilibrium, remains inefficient within the Boltzmann–Onsager framework. Driving electrons far from equilibrium broadens their energy spectrum and smears the Fermi edge, and this amplifies the temperature dependence of the electronic entropy. However, the hot-electron thermoelectric response beyond the classical thermal equilibrium limit has remained unexplored due to the lack of direct access to hot-electron dynamics. Here we image spatial distributions of electron and lattice temperatures together with the corresponding thermoelectric signals in HgTe and HgCdTe nanoconstrictions using coupled scanning-probe techniques. In HgTe, weak electron–phonon coupling allows hot electrons to remain far from thermal equilibrium with the lattice, and this generates large electron temperature gradients and a pronounced Thomson compensation effect. In HgCdTe the response shifts towards lattice-mediated heat redistribution due to the suppressed non-equilibrium state. These observations reveal a pronounced departure from the conventional near-equilibrium Boltzmann–Onsager expectations in high-field thermoelectricity, identify the Thomson effect as a key channel of non-equilibrium energy dissipation and establish a platform for exploring non-equilibrium thermoelectric phenomena in nanoscale conductors.

title: Motors use biased diffusion to shepherd diffusible proteins on microtubules
abstract: Far-from-equilibrium mixtures of active and passive molecules self-organize, but the principles remain unclear. Microtubules are cytoskeletal polymers composed of 13 protofilaments bound by mixtures of actively moving motors and passively diffusing microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs). They can serve as a model system for self-organization on a multi-lane lattice. Here we show that motors can shepherd diffusive MAPs along the lattice by rectifying Brownian motion into net directional drift without motor–MAP binding. Our model reveals that biased movement increases when fewer protofilaments are accessible or when lateral diffusion between protofilaments is limited, and identifies local dimensionality and diffusion as key parameters governing spatial patterning. In particular, shepherding depends on the total number of motors bound to the microtubules, and not on the individual motor processivity. We experimentally recapitulate micrometre-scale shepherding with a kinesin-1 motor (K401) and a diffusive MAP (PRC1), which show no detectable binding. These findings suggest shepherding is an emergent mechanism by which ensembles of motors generate micrometre-scale spatial patterning and transport of MAPs without direct binding interactions.

title: The challenge of recognition in large scientific collaborations
abstract: The authorship practices of large collaborations can hide individual contributions. A recognition programme developed by the LIGO Scientific Collaboration publicly documents verified contributions to research, infrastructure and community service.

title: Automated inverse design of metainterfaces with tailored friction laws
abstract: Providing dry solid contacts with on-demand macroscale frictional behaviour remains a formidable challenge in tribology, haptics and robotics. It has been shown that metainterfaces created from surfaces with engineered asperity-based topographies can achieve such friction control. However, only a few types of friction behaviour were demonstrated because suitable topographies were identified on the basis of human intuition. Here we introduce a numerical-optimization-based inverse design framework to automatically discover new metainterfaces that satisfy specified friction laws—relationships between friction and the normal force. To illustrate the framework’s versatility, we first expand the range of achievable friction coefficients for a given pair of materials. We next unlock friction laws showing power-law variation of frictional force with normal force, with exponents ranging between 2/3 and 1.35. We then achieve bilinear variation when the range of normal force is divided into segments, including cases for a smaller slope in the second segment than in the first. We validate relevant cases experimentally. Our automated framework enables systematic exploration of large parameter spaces, not limited to topography but potentially incorporating the individual asperities’ bulk material or surface physicochemistry. It offers design solutions for different friction laws and provides insights into the relationship between local interfacial properties and macroscopic friction.

title: Thermodynamic demonstration of tetracriticality and multicomponent superconductivity in UTe2
abstract: The candidate topological superconductor UTe 2 exhibits a complex phase diagram with multiple superconducting states, and the nature of their coexistence is not yet resolved. In particular, the apparent observation of two intersecting second-order phase boundaries at a triple point in the pressure–temperature phase diagram is thermodynamically forbidden. This suggests either a hidden phase transition or a fundamental misunderstanding of the superconductivity in this material. Here we observe an additional phase boundary that is characterized by an upward jump in the sound velocity. This is direct thermodynamic evidence for a phase transition in which superconducting order is lost on cooling. Our results establish a tetracritical point beyond which the ambient and pressure-induced superconducting order parameters form a multicomponent state. We use the measured phase diagram to demonstrate that strong competition between the two superconducting order parameters drives the loss of order when cooling, and leads to phase locking that suppresses superconducting fluctuations. These findings provide the definitive magnetic field–pressure–temperature phase diagram of UTe 2 and establish a thermodynamic foundation for multicomponent superconductivity.

title: Multiparticle quantum walks in a dipole-conserving Bose–Hubbard model
abstract: A strong potential gradient can localize individual particles in a crystal or optical lattice by making ordinary hopping energetically costly. Interactions can nevertheless enable correlated hopping processes that preserve the system’s centre of mass or, equivalently, its dipole moment. This constraint gives rise to fractonic behaviour, in which isolated excitations are immobile but their bound states can move. Here we realize individual mobile bound states of fractons in a dipole-conserving Bose–Hubbard model and observe their coherent quantum dynamics. Starting from a one-dimensional chain of ultracold bosonic atoms in an optical lattice, we use site-resolved optical potentials to deterministically generate localized dipole and antidipole excitations, which represent mobile bound states of a hole and a doublon. We track their individual quantum walks and characterize their strongly interacting scattering dynamics. Our study provides a bottom-up investigation of a Hamiltonian with kinetic constraints and offers an approach to exploring low-energy phases of fractonic matter.

title: Recent progress in the computational study of supercooled and glassy water
abstract: Computer simulation has become an essential tool for investigating the complex behaviour of cold, non-crystalline forms of water. In the past few years, improved computational capabilities, the use of advanced sampling algorithms and the rapid adoption of machine learning methods have driven major progress in the computational exploration of the properties of supercooled and glassy water. Here we review recent progress in this area, focusing on pure bulk water, and covering simulations of supercooled water using classical potentials, simulations of supercooled water using machine learning potentials and simulations of glassy water. The article selectively reviews work that, either methodologically or in its findings, has helped to define the current understanding of cold, disordered states of water that are metastable with respect to crystalline phases.
